subject: Economics
topic: Indian banking history II — mixed tiers
description: Bank nationalisation, Imperial Bank, SBI, RRBs, payment banks, recent mergers

questions.stem: FOURTEEN major commercial banks were nationalised in India in:

options.option_text: 1955, when SBI was formed from Imperial Bank
1969, by Indira Gandhi's bank nationalisation move
1991, with the major economic liberalisation reforms
2017, when SBI absorbed its associate banks formally

questions.explanation: First wave of bank nationalisation — 19 July 1969 by Indira Gandhi via the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Ordinance, 1969. 14 banks with deposits ≥ ₹50 crore each were nationalised. Aim: spread banking to rural areas + priority lending. Second wave — 1980, 6 more banks nationalised (deposit threshold ≥ ₹200 cr). Distractor 1 — SBI was formed in 1955 from Imperial Bank of India — distinct event. Distractor 3 — 1991 was liberalisation (allowed new private banks). Distractor 4 = SBI-associate merger.

questions.stem: The STATE BANK OF INDIA (SBI) was created in 1955 by transforming which earlier bank?

options.option_text: The Bank of Bengal, the oldest of three Presidency Banks
The Imperial Bank of India, formed in 1921
The Reserve Bank of India, founded in 1935
The Bank of Madras, one of three original Presidency Banks

questions.explanation: Imperial Bank of India formed 1921 by merging three Presidency Banks (Bank of Bengal, Bank of Bombay, Bank of Madras). Imperial Bank was India's de facto central bank till 1935 (when RBI took over). NATIONALISED + RENAMED as State Bank of India by SBI Act, 1955 — to expand banking in rural / semi-urban India. Now India's largest commercial bank: ~22,000 branches + ~58,000 ATMs. SBI also absorbed all 5 of its 'associate banks' (State Bank of Hyderabad, Mysore, Travancore, Patiala, Bikaner & Jaipur) and Bharatiya Mahila Bank in 2017.

questions.stem: REGIONAL RURAL BANKS (RRBs) were established in India under the:

options.option_text: Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 originally
Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976 by Indira Gandhi government
Banking Regulation Act, 1949 amended later
Co-operative Societies Act of various states then

questions.explanation: RRBs — established 26 September 1975 (first 5 RRBs); RRB Act, 1976 gave statutory basis. Aim: provide credit + banking facilities specifically to small farmers, agricultural labourers, artisans, small entrepreneurs in rural India. Capital structure: Centre 50%, sponsoring commercial bank 35%, State 15%. Currently ~43 RRBs (down from a peak of 196, due to mergers). Supervised by NABARD. Distractor 1 = covers RBI. Distractor 3 = covers commercial banks generally. Distractor 4 = covers cooperatives, separate.

questions.stem: PAYMENT BANKS — a special category introduced by RBI in 2015 — can:

options.option_text: Accept deposits without any limit and lend like other banks
Accept deposits up to ₹2 lakh (now) per customer but cannot lend
Operate exclusively in international markets and forex
Issue credit cards, like a regular commercial bank

questions.explanation: Payment Banks — a differentiated banking model. Can: accept deposits up to ₹2 lakh/customer (raised from ₹1 lakh in 2021); offer payment services + remittances; issue ATM/debit cards. CANNOT: lend or issue credit cards. Operational examples: India Post Payments Bank (IPPB), Airtel Payments Bank, Paytm Payments Bank (operations restricted by RBI in early 2024 due to compliance issues), Fino, NSDL. Aimed at financial inclusion of unbanked populations.

questions.stem: The MEGA BANK MERGER announced in August 2019 (effective April 2020) consolidated 10 PSU banks into:

options.option_text: 10 separate banks unchanged in structure
4 large banks for greater scale and efficiency
1 single mega public-sector banking entity
8 mid-sized banks for regional concentration

questions.explanation: 10 → 4 mergers (effective 1 April 2020): (1) Punjab National Bank + Oriental Bank of Commerce + United Bank → PNB. (2) Canara Bank + Syndicate Bank → Canara Bank. (3) Union Bank of India + Andhra Bank + Corporation Bank → Union Bank. (4) Indian Bank + Allahabad Bank → Indian Bank. Total PSU banks reduced from 27 (in 2017) to 12 today. Aim: stronger balance sheets, NPA management, scale economies, technology integration.

questions.stem: The first private-sector bank in India established AFTER the 1991 economic reforms was:

options.option_text: ICICI Bank, formed by merger of ICICI Ltd into a bank
UTI Bank (now Axis Bank) — first new private sector bank
Yes Bank, founded by Rana Kapoor in 2004
Kotak Mahindra Bank, originally a non-banking finance company

questions.explanation: 1991 reforms allowed new private-sector banks. UTI Bank — opened in 1994; renamed AXIS BANK in 2007. First in the post-reform private banking wave. Other early entrants: HDFC Bank (1994), ICICI Bank (1994 — initially as ICICI Banking Corporation; merged with ICICI Ltd 2002), IndusInd Bank (1994), GTB (Global Trust, later subsumed). Yes Bank (2004) and Kotak Mahindra (2003 — granted banking licence) came later. The first new bank licences to private sector in over 25 years (last had been in the 1960s).

questions.stem: BHARTIYA RESERVE BANK NOTE MUDRAN PRIVATE LIMITED (BRBNMPL), a printing press for Indian banknotes, was set up by the:

options.option_text: Government of India through the Finance Ministry
Reserve Bank of India as its wholly-owned subsidiary
Security Printing & Minting Corporation under Centre
Indian Banks' Association on a cooperative basis

questions.explanation: BRBNMPL — wholly-owned subsidiary of RBI, set up 1995. Two presses: MYSORE (Karnataka) and SALBONI (West Bengal). India's banknote printing capacity is split between RBI's BRBNMPL and the Centre's SPMCIL (Security Printing & Minting Corporation of India) — Nashik (Maharashtra) and Dewas (MP). All currency now is printed at one of these four locations. Coins minted at SPMCIL mints (Mumbai, Kolkata, Hyderabad, Noida). Distractor 1 — Centre owns SPMCIL not BRBNMPL. Distractor 3 — that's the OTHER printer. Distractor 4 — IBA is a banks' association, not a printer.

questions.stem: In the second wave of bank nationalisation in April 1980, the Government of India took over how many commercial banks, bringing the total public-sector bank count to twenty?

options.option_text: Four banks, taking the total PSB count to eighteen
Six banks, taking the total PSB count to twenty
Five banks, taking the total PSB count to nineteen
Eight banks, taking the total PSB count to twenty-two

questions.explanation: Six banks — Andhra Bank, Corporation Bank, New Bank of India, Oriental Bank of Commerce, Punjab & Sind Bank, and Vijaya Bank — were nationalised in April 1980 under Indira Gandhi's government. Added to the 14 banks nationalised in 1969, this brought the PSB total to 20. Option A (four) and C (five) are the commonest confusions; D (eight) overstates the 1980 wave.

questions.stem: NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development), established on 12 July 1982, was created in part by formally absorbing and winding up which earlier specialised institution?

options.option_text: Agricultural Finance Corporation (AFC), established 1963
Agricultural Refinance and Development Corporation (ARDC)
Industrial Finance Corporation of India (IFCI), founded 1948
National Cooperative Development Corporation (NCDC), 1963

questions.explanation: NABARD was formed by merging the Agricultural Refinance and Development Corporation (ARDC) into it and transferring the rural credit functions of the RBI's Agricultural Credit Department. ARDC (est. 1963) provided refinance to banks for farm loans; NABARD absorbed its entire operations in 1982. AFC (A) deals with agri-industry equity finance and was not merged. IFCI (C) and NCDC (D) are wholly unrelated to NABARD's creation.

questions.stem: The Imperial Bank of India, constituted in 1921 as the premier commercial bank of British India, was formed by amalgamating which three Presidency Banks?

options.option_text: Bank of Bengal, Bank of Bombay, and Bank of Punjab
Bank of Bengal, Bank of Bombay, and Bank of Madras
Bank of Bengal, Bank of Calcutta, and Bank of Madras
Bank of Bombay, Bank of Madras, and Bank of Mysore

questions.explanation: The Imperial Bank of India Act, 1920 merged the three Presidency Banks — Bank of Bengal (est. 1806), Bank of Bombay (est. 1840), and Bank of Madras (est. 1843) — effective 27 January 1921. Option C is the classic trap: there was no 'Bank of Calcutta'; the correct name was 'Bank of Bengal'. Option A substitutes 'Bank of Punjab', which was never a Presidency Bank; Option D adds 'Bank of Mysore', a princely-state institution entirely unconnected to this merger.

questions.stem: The LEAD BANK SCHEME — under which one nodal bank is assigned per district to anchor local credit planning — was introduced by RBI in December 1969 based on the recommendations of which body?

options.option_text: Gadgil Study Group on rural credit and banking expansion
F.K.D. Narimam Working Group on banking operations
Tandon Committee on working capital norms for banks
Chakravarty Committee on monetary system review

questions.explanation: The Lead Bank Scheme was formally recommended by the F.K.D. Narimam Working Group and implemented by RBI in December 1969, weeks after the July 1969 nationalisation. Option A (Gadgil Study Group) is the most tempting distractor: D.R. Gadgil did help conceptualise 'area banking' earlier, but the specific Lead Bank Scheme recommendation is attributed to Narimam. The Tandon Committee (C) dealt with working capital finance norms in 1974; the Chakravarty Committee (D) reviewed the monetary system in 1985.

questions.stem: Punjab National Bank (PNB), founded in Lahore in 1894 by Lala Lajpat Rai and Dayal Singh Majithia among others, occupies a unique place in Indian banking history primarily because it was the first bank to be:

options.option_text: Registered under Companies Act with no British directorship
Nationalised by the government in the first wave of 1969
Permitted to open branches across multiple provincial boundaries
Floated as a joint venture with the colonial government

questions.explanation: PNB is celebrated as India's first purely Swadeshi bank — incorporated under the Indian Companies Act with entirely Indian capital and an all-Indian board, free from any British directorship or Crown stake. This distinguished it from earlier banks such as the Bank of Bengal and Allahabad Bank, which had British participation. Option B is factually true (PNB was nationalised in 1969) but that is not its founding distinction. Options C and D describe conditions PNB did not hold exclusively or at all.

questions.stem: The DICGC deposit insurance ceiling of ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, announced in the Union Budget 2020–21, replaced an earlier limit that had remained frozen for 27 years since 1993. What was that frozen amount?

options.option_text: ₹50,000 per depositor per bank, set by 1968 amendment
₹1 lakh per depositor per bank, unchanged since 1993
₹2 lakh per depositor per bank, revised post-2008 crisis
₹25,000 per depositor per bank under the original 1961 Act

questions.explanation: DICGC's limit was raised from ₹30,000 (1980) to ₹1 lakh in 1993, where it remained for 27 years until the Finance Act 2020 raised it to ₹5 lakh — a change catalysed by the Punjab and Maharashtra Co-operative (PMC) Bank crisis of 2019. Option A (₹50,000) was the limit between 1976 and 1980, not the pre-2020 figure. Option C (₹2 lakh) is a fabrication with no historical basis. Option D (₹25,000) was the original limit at DICGC's inception in 1961. Candidates most often confuse the 1993 figure with either ₹50,000 or ₹2 lakh.

questions.stem: The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 significantly expanded RBI's powers of supersession, reconstruction, and amalgamation over which category of institutions previously governed primarily by state-level Registrars of Co-operative Societies?

options.option_text: Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) with assets above ₹500 crore
Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) for supersession and reconstruction
Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) with over 50% state government equity
Local Area Banks (LABs) operating across contiguous district clusters

questions.explanation: The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 empowered RBI to supersede the board of Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) and frame reconstruction or amalgamation schemes without the bank's consent — powers that existed for commercial banks but not UCBs. The PMC Bank crisis (2019) exposed this regulatory gap: UCBs were co-governed under state co-operative law, limiting RBI's ability to intervene early. NBFCs (A) operate under a separate RBI framework already. RRBs (C) are already subject to RBI/NABARD dual oversight. Local Area Banks (D) are a distinct small-bank licence category and were not the target of this amendment.
